title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (6 of 7)
hook: into blind darkness go those who follow ignorance, and into greater darkness those who follow knowledge alone
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (7 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekatva, oneness. The one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, stops shrinking back.

Two kinds of people can be hard to be around. One only cares about practical things: money, the schedule, what's for dinner, and never asks why. The other only cares about ideas: always reading, always explaining, and somehow never takes out the trash. Verses nine to fourteen of the Isha sound strange at first. They warn against something like both. And the warning for the second kind is harsher.
screen: `ONLY THE PRACTICAL.` → `ONLY THE IDEAS.` → `A WARNING FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Verse nine: into blind darkness enter those who follow avidya, not-knowing. Into a greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in vidya, knowing, alone. Knowledge, on its own, gets the worse darkness. What do the two words mean here? Vidya is knowledge, but Shankara takes it here as knowledge of the gods: meditation, inner study. Avidya, on his reading, is ritual action, work in the world, the practical side. Other teachers read the pair differently, and scholars still argue. The text itself doesn't define them. But it does say what to do with them. Verse eleven: the one who knows both together crosses death by avidya and gains the deathless by vidya. Not one or the other. Both, together. Verses twelve to fourteen run the same pattern with another pair: the manifest and the unmanifest, becoming and non-becoming. Again, those who follow only one go into darkness, and knowing both together is the way through. It fits the week. Verse two said keep working a hundred years. Verses six and seven spoke of seeing the one self. Here the Isha won't let you pick. Contemplation without action floats away. Action without contemplation gets lost. Renounce and enjoy has the same shape: two things that sound opposite, held in one hand. Doing the dishes and asking why you're alive belong in the same day.
screen: `BLIND DARKNESS: NOT-KNOWING ALONE.` · `GREATER DARKNESS: KNOWING ALONE.` · `KNOW BOTH TOGETHER.` · `CROSS DEATH, REACH THE DEATHLESS.` · then, large: `VIDYA AND AVIDYA, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Hold out both hands, palms up: in the left, put something practical waiting for you, an errand, a bill, a meal; in the right, one big question you carry, what matters, who you want to be. Feel both, don't drop either, and let both hands be equally heavy. When your mind leans to one side, bring it back to the middle.
Vidya, knowledge, from vid, to know. The one who knows both vidya and avidya together crosses death and gains the deathless; follow only one and it goes dark.
Your line: know both together. Either one, held alone, goes dark. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers of different schools read Isha verses 9–14 differently, but the verses are commonly taught as a call to hold inner knowledge and outer action together.

match.prompt: the paired opposites — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: you can follow knowing, or not-knowing. which way does the Isha point?
fork.reveal: both together. each alone leads into darkness; the knowledge-only path gets the greater one.

original.note: Sanskrit: vidya, knowledge; from vid, to know, the same root as Veda. Avidya is not-knowing.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowledge is always better than ignorance.
what it means: in these verses, knowing without doing leads into a darker place than doing without knowing.
what a scholar hears: 9–11 and 12–14 run the same three-verse pattern with vidya/avidya and sambhuti/asambhuti; Vedanta schools dispute the readings.
